stories.headline: Democrats lock in largest House majority since 1992 after Foxx loses recount
stories.summary: Democrat Chuck Hubbard defeated 11-term Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx in North Carolina after a recount, giving Democrats at least 258 House seats to Republicans' 173, the biggest majority either party has held after a national election in about three decades. Hakeem Jeffries, expected to become speaker in January, laid out priorities on affordability, health care and immigration and said there are areas where Democrats could work with President Trump.
stories.why_it_matters: A majority this large lets Democrats pass bills in the House without Republican votes and run investigations from January, which shapes what reaches the president on health care costs, spending and oversight of his administration.
stories.background: Democrats swept the Nov. 3 midterms, flipping dozens of Republican-held House seats; NPR described it as the biggest win for either party in 50 years. A handful of close races took weeks to settle, including Foxx's western North Carolina district, which went to a recount. Foxx chairs the House Rules Committee, which controls how bills reach the floor. Republicans keep control of the House only until the new Congress is sworn in in January, and they have about three weeks of session left to finish work such as a stopgap spending bill.

facts.text: Chuck Hubbard, a Democrat and retired journalist, defeated Rep. Virginia Foxx after a recount, according to projections by CBS News and NBC News.

Jeffries said Democrats would focus on affordability, expanding health care and fixing what he called a broken immigration system, and named areas where they could work with Trump.
House Republicans have about three weeks left in session before Democrats take over, with a stopgap funding measure at the top of their list, The Hill reported.
Before the final races were called, NPR reported that Democrats had flipped 46 Republican-held seats and called the result the largest win for either party in 50 years.

stories.headline: ICE arrest of father and daughter on Seattle jet bridge draws protests
stories.summary: Immigration officers in plain clothes detained a father and daughter on a jet bridge at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport on Saturday as they boarded an Alaska Airlines flight, and passenger video of the arrest spread widely. Washington state's leaders have repeatedly clashed with the administration over enforcement. Officers making arrests in unmarked clothing, sometimes masked, has become a flash point in several cities.

stories.headline: Army invokes emergency rule to detonate explosives in Iowa despite court order
stories.summary: The Army told a court it will use emergency provisions to detonate about five tons of unstable lead-based explosive material at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant near Middletown, going ahead despite a court order that had paused the plan. Environmental groups including the Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club's Iowa chapter sued over the permit, and a court paused the plan. The Army has now turned to an emergency exclusion to proceed.

stories.headline: Appeals court rules pregnant-worker accommodations law unconstitutional
stories.summary: A federal appeals court ruled that the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act, which requires employers to make reasonable accommodations for pregnant workers, is unconstitutional. The court said Congress passed it improperly because most House members were not physically present when it was approved in a December 2022 spending package. The decision is likely headed toward the Supreme Court.
stories.why_it_matters: The law guarantees pregnant workers changes like extra breaks, seating or lighter duty; the ruling puts those protections in doubt for workers covered by it and raises questions about other laws passed under pandemic-era proxy voting.
stories.background: Congress passed the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act in late 2022 as part of a large spending bill, while the House still allowed members to vote by proxy during the COVID-19 pandemic. Texas sued, arguing the Constitution requires a quorum of members to be physically present. A three-judge panel of the 5th Circuit upheld the law in August 2025, but the full court vacated that ruling in January 2026 and reheard the case. The challenge has so far concerned Texas as an employer.

facts.text: An appeals court ruled that the federal law requiring accommodations for pregnant workers is unconstitutional.
The court said the law was invalid because a majority of House members were not physically present when it passed as part of a December 2022 spending package.

At the May 2026 rehearing, conservative judges questioned the Justice Department's argument that physical presence was not required, Bloomberg Law reported.

stories.headline: UN climate talks in Turkey end without a deal after a fight over fossil fuels
stories.summary: The COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, collapsed on Sunday without a final agreement. About 130 parties, led by the EU, rejected the summit presidency's compromise text because it did not commit to moving away from fossil fuels. Countries now go home with no new collective plan. The next round of talks is a year away.
stories.why_it_matters: These yearly talks are the main place where governments agree to cut emissions and pay to cope with heat, floods and rising seas. With no deal, each country's existing promises stand, and those promises are not enough to meet the Paris targets.
stories.background: COP is the yearly conference of the nearly 200 countries in the UN climate treaty, which produced the 2015 Paris Agreement to limit warming. At COP28 in Dubai in 2023, countries agreed to transition away from fossil fuels, but last year's COP30 in Brazil ended without a roadmap for doing so. Turkey hosted COP31 under a compromise in which Australia chaired the negotiations. A draft published on Nov. 19 dropped references to ending fossil fuel use, and producer countries resisted firm new targets.

facts.text: The COP31 talks in Antalya ended on Sunday without a final agreement, after running two days past their scheduled close.
The BBC described the summit as the longest-running climate talks in UN history.

The EU, Panama and others, about 130 parties in all, refused to accept the COP president's consensus cover text, alleging it "greenwashes" fossil fuels, according to The Hindu. India, China and Saudi Arabia were on the other side of the divide.
Bloomberg reported that dozens of countries rejected a deal they saw as pandering to the fossil fuel industry.
Divisions over climate funding as well as fossil fuels kept almost 200 countries from reaching a deal, Daily Maverick reported.
It was the first time since the 2009 Copenhagen meeting that a COP failed to reach a final agreement, Reuters reported.
Pacific island nations said they were disappointed by the outcome, and in Australia there were calls for the minister who led the negotiations to resign.
A draft released on Nov. 19 had removed any reference to ending the use of fossil fuels.

stories.background: Since 2022 Ukraine has used remote-controlled sea drones to strike Russia's Black Sea Fleet and push it away from Ukrainian waters. This year the attacks have spread: in March, Russia blamed Ukrainian sea drones for sinking one of its tankers in the Mediterranean off Libya, and on Nov. 11 Ukraine said it hit a Russian missile ship in the Gulf of Finland. stories.headline: South Korea's education minister quits over AI cheating chaos at entrance exam

stories.headline: Stock futures bounce after the worst week for tech shares since 2020
stories.summary: US stock futures pointed to a strong rebound on Monday morning after last week's sell-off in artificial-intelligence stocks pushed the S&P 500 and the Dow into a correction. Coverage of the rebound in the digest came from center and left-leaning financial outlets; the one right-leaning item was a New York Post column questioning the bubble talk.
stories.background: For about three years, stock market gains have been led by companies that build or supply artificial intelligence, especially the chipmaker Nvidia. This month investors began to doubt that the hundreds of billions of dollars being spent on AI data centers will pay off, and they sold those shares heavily. A correction is a drop of at least 10 percent from a recent high. The selling deepened after Nvidia's chief executive, Jensen Huang, resigned on Nov. 12, and continued even after Nvidia's quarterly results and Anthropic's record stock market debut last week. This week is shortened by the Thanksgiving holiday.

stories.headline: Bond yields climb back as investors weigh another Fed rate increase
stories.summary: US Treasury yields rose on Monday, undoing part of last week's sharp drop, as investors moved money out of safe bonds and back toward stocks. Traders were waiting for a speech by New York Fed President John Williams, and the bank ING said upcoming economic data could support bets on another Federal Reserve rate increase. Investor Bill Ackman warned that a further hike could push the economy into recession.
stories.why_it_matters: Treasury yields set the baseline for mortgage, car-loan and credit-card rates, and CNBC reports that a spike in mortgage rates this fall has already frozen much of the housing market. Whether the Fed raises rates again in December will shape borrowing costs into next year.
stories.background: The Federal Reserve raises its benchmark interest rate to slow inflation, which has climbed back above 3.5 percent this year. It last raised rates in September, to a range of 3.75 to 4 percent, and markets have been betting on another increase at its December meeting. A Treasury yield is the interest the government pays to borrow; yields fall when investors rush into bonds for safety, as they did during last week's stock sell-off, and rise when that demand fades. John Williams, who leads the New York Fed, is one of the officials who votes on rates. Reports on economic growth and inflation are due later this week.

stories.headline: China, South Korea and Taiwan add emergency steps to steady stock markets
stories.summary: Regulators and stock exchange operators in China, South Korea and Taiwan rolled out new emergency measures to stop the slide in their markets caused by the global sell-off in AI stocks, The Wall Street Journal and CNBC reported. In Taiwan, margin calls on investors who borrowed to buy shares rose about 200-fold last week, according to Bloomberg.
stories.why_it_matters: Asian chipmakers supply the parts in most phones, computers and AI servers, so stress in these markets can spread to US stocks and to prices of electronics. Coverage came from center and left-leaning financial outlets.
stories.background: The stock markets of Taiwan, South Korea and China lean heavily on chipmakers and other suppliers to the AI industry, so they fell sharply when US tech shares dropped this month. Governments there have tools to slow a crash, such as stabilization funds that buy shares when prices fall fast and limits on short selling, which is betting that a share price will fall. A margin call is a demand from a broker that an investor who bought shares with borrowed money put up more cash or sell; many margin calls at once can force more selling. Taiwan's regulator first tightened short-selling rules on Nov. 6 and has since added more.

facts.text: Regulators and market operators in China, South Korea and Taiwan introduced new emergency measures to support their stock markets.

stories.headline: Mamdani releases 84,000 more 9/11 records as city portal tops 11 million visits
stories.summary: Mayor Zohran Mamdani and the city Law Department released another 84,000 records on Sunday about the Sept. 11 attacks and their aftermath, according to amNY and The Hill. amNY reports the release brings the total available to the public to more than 440,000 pages. The online portal for the records has drawn 11 million visits in two months, the Daily News and amNY report.
stories.why_it_matters: Tens of thousands of New Yorkers who lived, worked or volunteered near Ground Zero can now read what city officials knew about the air there. The records may matter to people pursuing 9/11 health claims.
stories.background: In September, on the attacks' 25th anniversary, the Mamdani administration opened a public portal with about 170,000 pages of city records on air quality and health after 9/11. The release followed a settlement with the advocacy group 9/11 Health Watch, and coverage at the time said the documents suggested officials knew the air was unsafe while telling the public otherwise. A second batch of 40,000 records followed in October. The city has said the Law Department will keep reviewing and posting records over the next year.

stories.summary: Police have charged a 25-year-old homeless man with murder in the death of a 62-year-old woman at her apartment on the edge of Chinatown, according to The New York Times and Gothamist. stories.headline: Hochul's office questions whether union leader Samuelsen lives in New York, putting his MTA board seat at risk
stories.summary: Gov. Kathy Hochul's office has told transit union leader John Samuelsen to prove he is a New York resident, City & State reports. Without that proof, his seat on the MTA board could be in jeopardy. The report comes from one outlet so far.
stories.why_it_matters: Samuelsen speaks for the workers who run the subways and buses on the board that sets fares and service. Losing his seat would remove a frequent critic of the governor from the board.
stories.background: John Samuelsen is international president of the Transport Workers Union of America and formerly led TWU Local 100, which represents most New York City subway and bus workers. He sits on the MTA board in a non-voting seat recommended by the union and traditionally held by organized labor. He has often clashed with Hochul, including over congestion pricing and transit contracts. State law sets residency requirements for MTA board members, and those rules have been contested for past nominees.

stories.headline: Open-primary group files 75,000 petitions despite opposition from Mamdani
stories.summary: The group Unite NY filed 75,000 petitions seeking to bring open primaries to New York City elections, the New York Post reports. The Post says Mayor Zohran Mamdani and City Hall oppose the effort. The measure would let voters not enrolled in a party take part in primaries.
stories.why_it_matters: New Yorkers not enrolled in a party cannot vote in the primaries that usually decide city races, and this measure aims to change that. So far only the right-leaning Post has reported the new filing.
stories.background: New York has closed primaries: only voters registered with a party can vote in its primary. In a city where Democrats dominate, that means many unaffiliated voters have no real say in who wins. In July, Unite NY delivered more than 45,000 signatures to the city clerk, enough to send the proposal to the City Council, and said it could gather more to reach the ballot if the Council did not act.

stories.headline: Antipoverty groups urge Albany to replace stolen SNAP benefits before Thanksgiving
stories.summary: Antipoverty groups are calling on the state to replace food stamp benefits stolen from New Yorkers' cards, THE CITY reports. The story features a Bensonhurst family whose monthly benefits were stolen last holiday season. Advocates are making the push as Thanksgiving approaches.
stories.why_it_matters: Thieves have drained food aid from low-income families' cards, in some cases taking a whole month's benefits. Since federal reimbursement ended, those families generally have not been repaid.
stories.background: SNAP benefits sit on electronic cards that thieves have copied with skimming devices at store checkout machines. The federal government stopped paying to replace skimmed benefits at the end of 2024, leaving it to states to decide whether to use their own money. Gov. Kathy Hochul has announced chip-enabled benefit cards, which are harder to copy, starting in early 2027. Advocates say families hit in the meantime still need to be repaid.

markets.summary: U.S. stocks had a rough week: the Nasdaq fell about 10%, its worst week since early 2020, and the S&P 500 and Dow both ended in a correction, meaning a drop of 10% or more from a recent high, as investors sold artificial-intelligence shares. Much of the pressure centered on Nvidia, which has been without its longtime chief executive since Jensen Huang resigned this month amid a scandal over his relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence contact. Stock futures pointed to a rebound on Monday morning, led by battered AI names, after President Trump urged Nvidia's board to bring Huang back, and regulators in China, South Korea and Taiwan added emergency steps to steady their markets. Treasury yields, the interest rates the government pays to borrow, rose Monday as money moved out of safe bonds, and investors are listening to New York Fed President John Williams for hints of another Fed rate increase. With the 10-year yield just above 5%, the average 30-year mortgage rate sits near 7.3%.

concept.explanation: A bubble is when prices of an asset climb far above what the underlying businesses are likely to earn, driven mostly by investors expecting prices to keep rising. Bubbles deflate when that expectation breaks: a disappointing earnings report, higher interest rates or a scandal can make buyers step back, and falling prices then push others to sell. Whether AI stocks were in one is debated, which is why last week's sharp drop and Monday's bounce draw so much attention. For ordinary people the effect shows up in retirement accounts and index funds, which hold large stakes in big tech companies, and in hiring plans when those companies' shares fall.
